newsitem.title: USA: G7 offers $300 million to bury Chernobyl shell.
newsitem.headline: G7 offers $300 million to bury Chernobyl shell.

text.p: The Group of Seven rich nations on Saturday urged Ukraine to step up the pace of economic reforms and promised $300 million to help rebuild the concrete shell round the ruined Chernobyl nuclear reactor.
A draft of a G7 statement to be released later on Saturday said the Chernobyl reactor, scene of the world's worst nuclear accident, should be closed completely by the year 2000.
"We reaffirm our commitment to assist Ukraine...in mobilising funds for energy projects to help meet its power needs in 2000 and beyond after Chernobyl's closure," the statement said.
"We endorse the setting up of a multilateral funding mechanism (to build a new shell) and have agreed that the G7 will contribute $300 million over the lifetime of the project."

The G7, worried about the state of the cracked concrete "sarcophagus" thrown up hurridly around the Chernobyl reactor after it exploded in 1986, has been urging Ukraine for years to close the station.
Kiev says it can only do so when new reactors have been built at other plants. It wants $780 million to help build a new sarcophagus.
Something under half of that had been expected to come from the G7 nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
G7 ministers are also concerned about sluggish Ukrainian economic reforms. In a toughly worded statement, they urged Kiev to step up the pace and encourage foreign investors.
"We encourage Ukraine to tackle the challenges of reinvigorating economic reform and creating a more welcoming environment for investors," the statement said.

"Immediate progress on the ambitious reform plan outlined by the Ukrainian government last fall is crucial to that effort and to gaining access to the considerable financing package already available."
The G7 statement described building a new tomb for the Chernobyl reactor as an expensive project and "a major challenge for the international community".
It said a special donor conference should be held this fall to decide how to fund the reconstruction work on the shell, which covers some 200 tonnes of highly radioactive concrete and nuclear fuel.

It was the second time in two months that the G7 had urged Kiev to implement its ambitious reform programme. Finance Ministers and central bank chiefs said in April they were growing increasingly worried and reforms were needed soon.
